A name formerly given in Pennsylvania, Maryland, and Virginia to the Spanish real of one eighth of a dollar (or 12½ cents), valued at eleven pence when the dollar was rated at 7s. 6d.

Levy.etym: [A contr. of elevenpence or elevenpenny bit.]

senses.d: The act of levying or collecting by authority; as, the levy of troops, taxes, etc.
q: A levy of all the men left under sixty.

senses.d: That which is levied, as an army, force, tribute, etc.
The taking or seizure of property on executions to satisfy judgments, or on warrants for the collection of taxes; a collecting by execution.

Levy.etym: [F. levée, fr. lever to raise. See Lever, and cf. Levee.]

senses.d: To raise, as a siege.
To raise; to collect; said of troops, to form into an army by enrollment, conscription, etc.
q: Augustine . . . inflamed Ethelbert, king of Kent, to levy his power, and to war against them.

senses.d: To raise or collect by assessment; to exact by authority; as, to levy taxes, toll, tribute, or contributions.
q: If they do this . . . my ransom, then, Will soon be levied.

senses.d: To gather or exact; as, to levy money.
To seize property, real or personal, or subject it to the operation of an execution; to make a levy; as, to levy on property; the usual mode of levying, in England, is by seizing the goods.
Not clerical; laic; laical; hence, unlearned; simple.
q: For if a priest be foul, on whom we trust, No wonder is a lewed man to rust.
So these great clerks their little wisdom show To mock the lewd, as learn'd in this as they.

senses.d: Belonging to the lower classes, or the rabble; idle and lawless; bad; vicious.
q: But the Jews, which believed not, . . . took unto them certain lewd fellows of the baser sort, . . . and assaulted the house of Jason.
Too lewd to work, and ready for any kind of mischief.

senses.d: Given to the promiscuous indulgence of lust; dissolute; lustful; libidinous.
Suiting, or proceeding from, lustfulness; involving unlawful sexual desire; as, lewd thoughts, conduct, or language.

Lewd.syn: Lustful; libidinous; licentious; profligate; dissolute; sensual; unchaste; impure; lascivious; lecherous; rakish; debauched.
Lewd.etym: [OE. lewed, lewd, lay, ignorant, vile, AS. lǣwed laical, belonging to the laity.]

senses.d: A Chinese measure of distance, being a little more than one third of a mile.
A Chinese copper coin; a cash. See Cash.
A person who knowingly utters falsehood; one who lies.
Free by birth; hence, befitting a freeman or gentleman; refined; noble; independent; free; not servile or mean; as, a liberal ancestry; a liberal spirit; liberal arts or studies.
Bestowing in a large and noble way, as a freeman; generous; bounteous; open-handed; as, a liberal giver.
q: Infinitely good, and of his good As liberal and free as infinite.

senses.d: Bestowed in a large way; hence, more than sufficient; abundant; bountiful; ample; profuse; as, a liberal gift; a liberal discharge of matter or of water.
q: His wealth doth warrant a liberal dower.

senses.d: Not strict or rigorous; not confined or restricted to the literal sense; free; as, a liberal translation of a classic, or a liberal construction of law or of language.
Not narrow or contracted in mind; not selfish; enlarged in spirit; catholic.
Free to excess; regardless of law or moral restraint; licentious.

Not bound by orthodox tenets or established forms in political or religious philosophy; independent in opinion; not conservative; friendly to great freedom in the constitution or administration of government; having tendency toward democratic or republican, as distinguished from monarchical or aristocratic, forms; as, liberal thinkers; liberal Christians; the Liberal party.
q: I confess I see nothing liberal in this “ order of thoughts,” as Hobbes elsewhere expresses it.

Liberal.syn: Generous; bountiful; munificent; beneficent; ample; large; profuse; free.
Liberal.etym: [F. libéral, L. liberalis, from liber free; perh. akin to libet, lubet, it pleases, E. lief. Cf. Deliver.]

senses.d: One who favors greater freedom in political or religious matters; an opponent of the established systems; a reformer; in English politics, a member of the Liberal party, so called. Cf. Whig.
The quality or state of being liberal; liberal disposition or practice; freedom from narrowness or prejudice; generosity; candor; charity.
q: That liberality is but cast away Which makes us borrow what we can not pay.

senses.d: A gift; a gratuity; — sometimes in the plural; as, a prudent man is not impoverished by his liberalities.
In a liberal manner.
A manumitted slave; a freedman; also, the son of a freedman.
One of a sect of Anabaptists, in the fifteenth and early part of the sixteenth century, who rejected many of the customs and decencies of life, and advocated a community of goods and of women.
One free from restraint; one who acts according to his impulses and desires; now, specifically, one who gives rein to lust; a rake; a debauchee.
q: Like a puffed and reckless libertine, Himself the primrose path of dalliance treads.

senses.d: A defamatory name for a freethinker.

Libertine.etym: [L. libertinus freedman, from libertus one made free, fr. liber free: cf. F. libertin. See Liberal.]

senses.d: Free from restraint; uncontrolled.
q: You are too much libertine.

senses.d: Dissolute; licentious; profligate; loose in morals; as, libertine principles or manners.

Libertine.etym: [L. libertinus of a freedman: cf. F. libertin. See Libertine, n. ]

senses.d: The state of a free person; exemption from subjection to the will of another claiming ownership of the person or services; freedom; — opposed to slavery, serfdom, bondage, or subjection.
q: But ye . . . caused every man his servant, and every man his handmaid whom he had set at liberty at their pleasure, to return, and brought them into subjection.
Delivered fro the bondage of corruption into the glorious liberty of the sons of God.

senses.d: Freedom from imprisonment, bonds, or other restraint upon locomotion.
q: Being pent from liberty, as I am now.

senses.d: A privilege conferred by a superior power; permission granted; leave; as, liberty given to a child to play, or to a witness to leave a court, and the like.
Privilege; exemption; franchise; immunity enjoyed by prescription or by grant; as, the liberties of the commercial cities of Europe.
q: His majesty gave not an entire county to any; much less did he grant . . . any extraordinary liberties.

senses.d: The place within which certain immunities are enjoyed, or jurisdiction is exercised.
q: Brought forth into some public or open place within the liberty of the city, and there . . . burned.

senses.d: A certain amount of freedom; permission to go freely within certain limits; also, the place or limits within which such freedom is exercised; as, the liberties of a prison.
A privilege or license in violation of the laws of etiquette or propriety; as, to permit, or take, a liberty.
q: He was repeatedly provoked into striking those who had taken liberties with him.

senses.d: The power of choice; freedom from necessity; freedom from compulsion or constraint in willing.
q: The idea of liberty is the idea of a power in any agent to do or forbear any particular action, according to the determination or thought of the mind, whereby either of them is preferred to the other.
This liberty of judgment did not of necessity lead to lawlessness.

senses.d: A curve or arch in a bit to afford room for the tongue of the horse.
Leave of absence; permission to go on shore.

Liberty.etym: [OE. liberte, F. liberté, fr. L. libertas, fr. liber free. See Liberal.]

senses.d: Of or pertaining to Libya, the ancient name of that part of Africa between Egypt and the Atlantic Ocean, or of Africa as a whole.
To draw or pass the tongue over; as, a dog licks his master's hand.
To lap; to take in with the tongue; as, a dog or cat licks milk.

Lick.etym: [AS. liccian; akin to OS. likkōn, D. likken, OHG. lecchōn, G. lecken, Goth. bi-laigōn, Russ. lizate, L. lingere, Gr. λείχειν , Skr. lih, rih. √121. Cf. Lecher, Relish.]

senses.d: A stroke of the tongue in licking.

A quick and careless application of anything, as if by a stroke of the tongue, or of something which acts like a tongue; as, to put on colors with a lick of the brush. Also, a small quantity of any substance so applied.
q: A lick of court whitewash.

senses.d: A place where salt is found on the surface of the earth, to which wild animals resort to lick it up; — often, but not always, near salt springs.
To strike with repeated blows for punishment; to flog; to whip or conquer, as in a pugilistic encounter.

Lick.etym: [Cf. OSw. lägga to place, strike, prick.]

senses.d: A slap; a quick stroke.
That which covers the opening of a vessel or box, etc.; a movable cover; as, the lid of a chest or trunk.
The cover of the eye; an eyelid.
q: Tears, big tears, gushed from the rough soldier's lid.

senses.d: The cover of the spore cases of mosses.

Lid.etym: [AS. hlid, fr. hlīdan (in comp.) to cover, shut; akin to OS. hlīdan (in comp.), D. lid lid, OHG. hlit, G. augenlid eyelid, Icel. hlið gate, gateway. √40.]

senses.d: A falsehood uttered or acted for the purpose of deception; an intentional violation of truth; an untruth spoken with the intention to deceive.
q: The proper notion of a lie is an endeavoring to deceive another by signifying that to him as true, which we ourselves think not to be so.
It is willful deceit that makes a lie. A man may act a lie, as by pointing his finger in a wrong direction when a traveler inquires of him his road.

senses.d: A fiction; a fable; an untruth.
Anything which misleads or disappoints.
q: Wishing this lie of life was o'er.

Lie.etym: [AS. lyge; akin to D. leugen, OHG. lugi, G. lüge, lug, Icel. lygi, Dan. & Sw. lögn, Goth. liugn. See Lie to utter a falsehood.]

senses.d: To utter falsehood with an intention to deceive; to say or do that which is intended to deceive another, when he a right to know the truth, or when morality requires a just representation.

Lie.etym: [OE. lien, li”en, le”en, leo”en, AS. leógan; akin to D. liegen, OS. & OHG. liogan, G. lügen, Icel. ljūga, Sw. ljuga, Dan. lyve, Goth. liugan, Russ. lgate.]

senses.d: To rest extended on the ground, a bed, or any support; to be, or to put one's self, in an horizontal position, or nearly so; to be prostate; to be stretched out; — often with down, when predicated of living creatures; as, the book lies on the table; the snow lies on the roof; he lies in his coffin.
q: The watchful traveler . . . Lay down again, and closed his weary eyes.

senses.d: To be situated; to occupy a certain place; as, Ireland lies west of England; the meadows lie along the river; the ship lay in port.

To abide; to remain for a longer or shorter time; to be in a certain state or condition; as, to lie waste; to lie fallow; to lie open; to lie hid; to lie grieving; to lie under one's displeasure; to lie at the mercy of the waves; the paper does not lie smooth on the wall.
To be or exist; to belong or pertain; to have an abiding place; to consist; — with in.
q: Envy lies between beings equal in nature, though unequal in circumstances.
He that thinks that diversion may not lie in hard labor, forgets the early rising and hard riding of huntsmen.

senses.d: To lodge; to sleep.
q: Whiles I was now trifling at home, I saw London, . . . where I lay one night only.
Mr. Quinion lay at our house that night.

senses.d: To be still or quiet, like one lying down to rest.
q: The wind is loud and will not lie.

senses.d: To be sustainable; to be capable of being maintained.

Lie.etym: [OE. lien, liggen, AS. licgan; akin to D. liggen, OHG. ligen, licken, G. liegen, Icel. liggja, Sw. ligga, Dan. ligge, Goth. ligan, Russ. lejate, L. lectus bed, Gr. λέχοσ bed, λέξασθαι to lie. Cf. Lair, Law, Lay, v. t., Litter, Low, adj.]

senses.d: The position or way in which anything lies; the lay, as of land or country.
q: He surveyed with his own eyes . . . the lie of the country on the side towards Thrace.

senses.d: A lay; a German song. It differs from the French chanson, and the Italian canzone, all three being national.
q: The German Lied is perhaps the most faithful reflection of the national sentiment.

senses.d: A legal claim; a charge upon real or personal property for the satisfaction of some debt or duty; a right in one to control or hold and retain the property of another until some claim of the former is paid or satisfied.

Lien.etym: [F. lien band, bond, tie, fr. L. ligamen, fr. ligare to bind. Cf. League a union, Leam a string, Leamer, Ligament.]

senses.d: One who lies down; one who rests or remains, as in concealment.
q: There were liers in ambush against him.

senses.d: An officer who supplies the place of a superior in his absence; a representative of, or substitute for, another in the performance of any duty.
q: The lawful magistrate, who is the vicegerent or lieutenant of God.

senses.d: A commissioned officer in the army, next below a captain.

Lieutenant.etym: [F., fr. lieu place + tenant holding, p. pr. of tenir to hold, L. tenere. See Lieu, and Tenant, and cf. Locum Tenens.]

senses.d: The state of being which begins with generation, birth, or germination, and ends with death; also, the time during which this state continues; that state of an animal or plant in which all or any of its organs are capable of performing all or any of their functions; — used of all animal and vegetable organisms.
Of human beings: The union of the soul and body; also, the duration of their union; sometimes, the deathless quality or existence of the soul; as, man is a creature having an immortal life.
q: She shows a body rather than a life.

senses.d: The potential principle, or force, by which the organs of animals and plants are started and continued in the performance of their several and coöperative functions; the vital force, whether regarded as physical or spiritual.

Figuratively: The potential or animating principle, also, the period of duration, of anything that is conceived of as resembling a natural organism in structure or functions; as, the life of a state, a machine, or a book; authority is the life of government.

A certain way or manner of living with respect to conditions, circumstances, character, conduct, occupation, etc.; hence, human affairs; also, lives, considered collectively, as a distinct class or type; as, low life; a good or evil life; the life of Indians, or of miners.
q: That which before us lies in daily life.
By experience of life abroad in the world.
Lives of great men all remind us We can make our lives sublime.
'T is from high life high characters are drawn.

senses.d: Animation; spirit; vivacity; vigor; energy.
q: No notion of life and fire in fancy and in words.
That gives thy gestures grace and life.

senses.d: That which imparts or excites spirit or vigor; that upon which enjoyment or success depends; as, he was the life of the company, or of the enterprise.
The living or actual form, person, thing, or state; as, a picture or a description from the life.
A person; a living being, usually a human being; as, many lives were sacrificed.
The system of animal nature; animals in general, or considered collectively.
q: Full nature swarms with life.

senses.d: An essential constituent of life, esp. the blood.
q: The words that I speak unto you . . . they are life.
The warm life came issuing through the wound.

senses.d: A history of the acts and events of a life; a biography; as, Johnson wrote the life of Milton.

Life.etym: [AS. līf; akin to D. lijf body, G. leib body, MHG. līp life, body, OHG. līb life, Icel. līf, life, body, Sw. lif, Dan. liv, and E. live, v. √119. See Live, and cf. Alive.]

senses.d: The time that life continues.
The sky; the atmosphere; the firmament.

To move in a direction opposite to that of gravitation; to raise; to elevate; to bring up from a lower place to a higher; to upheave; sometimes implying a continued support or holding in the higher place; — said of material things; as, to lift the foot or the hand; to lift a chair or a burden.
To raise, elevate, exalt, improve, in rank, condition, estimation, character, etc.; — often with up.
q: The Roman virtues lift up mortal man.
Lest, being lifted up with pride.

senses.d: To bear; to support.
To collect, as moneys due; to raise.
To steal; to carry off by theft (esp. cattle); as, to lift a drove of cattle.
q: He ne'er lift up his hand but conquered.

Lift.etym: [Icel. lypta, fr. lopt air; akin to Sw. lyfta to lift, Dan. löfte, G. lüften; — prop., to raise into the air. See Loft, and cf. 1st Lift.]

senses.d: To try to raise something; to exert the strength for raising or bearing.
q: Strained by lifting at a weight too heavy.

senses.d: To rise; to become or appear raised or elevated; as, the fog lifts; the land lifts to a ship approaching it.
To live by theft.
Act of lifting; also, that which is lifted.
The space or distance through which anything is lifted; as, a long lift.
Help; assistance, as by lifting; as, to give one a lift in a wagon.
q: The goat gives the fox a lift.

senses.d: That by means of which a person or thing lifts or is lifted
A rise; a degree of elevation; as, the lift of a lock in canals.
A lift gate. See Lift gate, below.
A rope leading from the masthead to the extremity of a yard below; — used for raising or supporting the end of the yard.
One of the steps of a cone pulley.
A layer of leather in the heel.
That portion of the vibration of a balance during which the impulse is given.
One who, or that which, lifts.
A tool for lifting loose sand from the mold; also, a contrivance attached to a cope, to hold the sand together when the cope is lifted.
Used in, or for, or by, lifting.
That agent, force, or action in nature by the operation of which upon the organs of sight, objects are rendered visible or luminous.
That which furnishes, or is a source of, light, as the sun, a star, a candle, a lighthouse, etc.
q: Then he called for a light, and sprang in.
And God made two great lights; the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night.

senses.d: The time during which the light of the sun is visible; day; especially, the dawn of day.
q: The murderer, rising with the light, killeth the poor and needy.

senses.d: The brightness of the eye or eyes.
q: He seemed to find his way without his eyes; For out o' door he went without their helps, And, to the last, bended their light on me.

senses.d: The medium through which light is admitted, as a window, or window pane; a skylight; in architecture, one of the compartments of a window made by a mullion or mullions.
q: There were windows in three rows, and light was against light in three ranks.

senses.d: Life; existence.
q: O, spring to light, auspicious Babe, be born!

senses.d: Open view; a visible state or condition; public observation; publicity.
q: The duke yet would have dark deeds darkly answered; he would never bring them to light.

senses.d: The power of perception by vision.
q: My strength faileth me; as for the light of my eyes, it also is gone from me.

senses.d: That which illumines or makes clear to the mind; mental or spiritual illumination; enlightenment; knowledge; information.
q: He shall never know That I had any light of this from thee.

senses.d: Prosperity; happiness; joy; felicity.
q: Then shall thy light break forth as the morning, and thy health shall spring forth speedily.

senses.d: The manner in which the light strikes upon a picture; that part of a picture which represents those objects upon which the light is supposed to fall; the more illuminated part of a landscape or other scene; — opposed to shade. Cf. Chiaroscuro.
Appearance due to the particular facts and circumstances presented to view; point of view; as, to state things fairly and put them in the right light.
q: Frequent consideration of a thing . . . shows it in its several lights and various ways of appearance.

Light.etym: [OE. light, liht, AS. leóht; akin to OS. lioht, D. & G. licht, OHG. lioht, Goth. liuhaþ, Icel. ljōs, L. lux light, lucere to shine, Gr. λευκόσ white, Skr. ruc to shine. √122. Cf. Lucid, Lunar, Luminous, Lynx.]

senses.d: Having light; not dark or obscure; bright; clear; as, the apartment is light.
White or whitish; not intense or very marked; not of a deep shade; moderately colored; as, a light color; a light brown; a light complexion.
To set fire to; to cause to burn; to set burning; to ignite; to kindle; as, to light a candle or lamp; to light the gas; — sometimes with up.
q: If a thousand candles be all lighted from one.
And the largest lamp is lit.
Absence might cure it, or a second mistress Light up another flame, and put out this.

senses.d: To give light to; to illuminate; to fill with light; to spread over with light; — often with up.
q: Ah, hopeless, lasting flames ! like those that burn To light the dead.
One hundred years ago, to have lit this theater as brilliantly as it is now lighted would have cost, I suppose, fifty pounds.
The sun has set, and Vesper, to supply His absent beams, has lighted up the sky.

senses.d: To attend or conduct with a light; to show the way to by means of a light.
q: His bishops lead him forth, and light him on.

Light.etym: [AS. lȳhtan, līhtan, to shine. √122. See Light, n.]

senses.d: To become ignited; to take fire; as, the match will not light.
To be illuminated; to receive light; to brighten; — with up; as, the room lights up very well.
Having little, or comparatively little, weight; not tending to the center of gravity with force; not heavy.
q: These weights did not exert their natural gravity, . . . insomuch that I could not guess which was light or heavy whilst I held them in my hand.

senses.d: Not burdensome; easy to be lifted, borne, or carried by physical strength; as, a light burden, or load.
q: Ye shall find rest unto your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.

senses.d: Easy to be endured or performed; not severe; not difficult; as, a light affliction or task.
q: Light sufferings give us leisure to complain.

senses.d: Easy to be digested; not oppressive to the stomach; as, light food; also, containing little nutriment.
Not heavily armed; armed with light weapons; as, light troops; a troop of light horse.
Not encumbered; unembarrassed; clear of impediments; hence, active; nimble; swift.
q: Unmarried men are best friends, best masters . . . but not always best subjects, for they are light to run away.

senses.d: Not heavily burdened; not deeply laden; not sufficiently ballasted; as, the ship returned light.
Slight; not important; as, a light error.
Well leavened; not heavy; as, light bread.
Not copious or heavy; not dense; not inconsiderable; as, a light rain; a light snow; light vapors.
Not strong or violent; moderate; as, a light wind.
Not pressing heavily or hard upon; hence, having an easy, graceful manner; delicate; as, a light touch; a light style of execution.

Light.etym: [OE. light, liht, AS. līht, leóht; akin to D. ligt, G. leicht, OHG. līhti, Icel. lēttr, Dan. let, Sw. lätt, Goth. leihts, and perh. to L. levis (cf. Levity), Gr. ελαχὔσ small, Skr. laghu light. √125. ]

senses.d: Lightly; cheaply.
To lighten; to ease of a burden; to take off.
q: From his head the heavy burgonet did light.

Light.etym: [See Light not heavy, and cf. Light to alight, and Lighten to make less heavy.]

senses.d: To dismount; to descend, as from a horse or carriage; to alight; — with from, off, on, upon, at, in.
q: When she saw Isaac, she lighted off the camel.
Slowly rode across a withered heath, And lighted at a ruined inn.

senses.d: To feel light; to be made happy.
q: It made all their hearts to light.

senses.d: To descend from flight, and rest, perch, or settle, as a bird or insect.
q: lights on that, and this, and tasteth all.
On the tree tops a crested peacock lit.

senses.d: To come down suddenly and forcibly; to fall; — with on or upon.
q: On me, me only, as the source and spring Of all corruption, all the blame lights due.

senses.d: To come by chance; to happen; — with on or upon; formerly with into.
q: The several degrees of vision, which the assistance of glasses (casually at first lit on) has taught us to conceive.
They shall light into atheistical company.
And here we lit on Aunt Elizabeth, And Lilia with the rest.

Light.etym: [AS. līhtan to alight, orig., to relieve (a horse) of the rider's burden, to make less heavy, fr. līht light. See Light not heavy, and cf. Alight, Lighten to make light.]

senses.d: To descend; to light.
q: O Lord, let thy mercy lighten upon us.

senses.d: To burst forth or dart, as lightning; to shine with, or like, lightning; to display a flash or flashes of lightning; to flash.
q: This dreadful night, That thunders, lightens, opens graves, and roars As doth the lion.

senses.d: To grow lighter; to become less dark or lowering; to brighten; to clear, as the sky.

Lighten.etym: [OE. lightenen. See Light to kindle, illuminate.]

senses.d: To make light or clear; to light; to illuminate; as, to lighten an apartment with lamps or gas; to lighten the streets.
q: A key of fire ran all along the shore, And lightened all the river with a blaze.

senses.d: To illuminate with knowledge; to enlighten.
q: Lighten my spirit with one clear heavenly ray.

senses.d: To emit or disclose in, or as in, lightning; to flash out, like lightning.
q: His eye . . . lightens forth Controlling majesty.

senses.d: To free from trouble and fill with joy.
q: They looked unto him, and were lightened.

senses.d: To make lighter, or less heavy; to reduce in weight; to relieve of part of a load or burden; as, to lighten a ship by unloading; to lighten a load or burden.
To make less burdensome or afflictive; to alleviate; as, to lighten the cares of life or the burden of grief.
To cheer; to exhilarate.
q: Lightens my humor with his merry jests.

senses.d: One who, or that which, lights; as, a lighter of lamps.
A large boat or barge, mainly used in unloading or loading vessels which can not reach the wharves at the place of shipment or delivery.

Lighter.etym: [D. ligter, fr. ligt light. See Light not heavy.]

senses.d: To convey by a lighter, as to or from the shore; as, to lighter the cargo of a ship.
A name sometimes applied to the process of annealing metals.
With little weight; with little force; as, to tread lightly; to press lightly.
q: Yet shall thy grave with rising flowers be drest, And the green turf lie lightly on thy breast.
Him thus intent Ithuriel with his spear Touched lightly.

senses.d: Swiftly; nimbly; with agility.
q: So mikle was that barge, it might not lightly sail.
Watch what thou seest and lightly bring me word.

senses.d: Without deep impression.
q: The soft ideas of the cheerful note, Lightly received, were easily forgot.

senses.d: In a small degree; slightly; not severely.
q: At the first he lightly afflicted the land of Zebulun . . . and afterward did more grievously afflict her.

senses.d: With little effort or difficulty; easily; readily.
q: That lightly come, shall lightly go.
They come lightly by the malt, and need not spare it.

senses.d: Without reason, or for reasons of little weight.
q: Flatter not the rich, neither do thou willingly or lightly appear before great personages.

senses.d: Commonly; usually.
q: The great thieves of a state are lightly the officers of the crown.

senses.d: Without dejection; cheerfully.
Without heed or care; with levity; gayly; airily.
q: Matrimony . . . is not by any to be enterprised, nor taken in hand, unadvisedly, lightly, or wantonly.

senses.d: Not chastely; wantonly.
The state, condition, or quality, of being light or not heavy; buoyancy; levity; fickleness; nimbleness; delicacy; grace.

Lightness.syn: Levity; volatility; instability; inconstancy; unsteadiness; giddiness; flightiness; airiness; gayety; liveliness; agility; nimbleness; sprightliness; briskness; swiftness; ease; facility.

senses.d: Illumination, or degree of illumination; as, the lightness of a room.
Absence of depth or of duskiness in color; as, the lightness of a tint; lightness of complexion.

A discharge of atmospheric electricity, accompanied by a vivid flash of light, commonly from one cloud to another, sometimes from a cloud to the earth. The sound produced by the electricity in passing rapidly through the atmosphere constitutes thunder.
The act of making bright, or the state of being made bright; enlightenment; brightening, as of the mental powers.
Lightening.
The lungs of an animal or bird; — sometimes coarsely applied to the lungs of a human being.
A kind of precious stone.
q: The third row a ligure, an agate, and an amethyst.

Ligure.etym: [L. ligurius, Gr. λιγύριον, λιγγούριον, λιγκούριον, λυγκούριον, equiv. to Heb. leshem.]

senses.d: Having the same, or nearly the same, appearance, qualities, or characteristics; resembling; similar to; similar; alike; — often with in and the particulars of the resemblance; as, they are like each other in features, complexion, and many traits of character.
q: 'T is as like you As cherry is to cherry.
Like master, like man.
He giveth snow like wool; he scattereth the hoar-frost like ashes.

senses.d: Equal, or nearly equal; as, fields of like extent.
q: More clergymen were impoverished by the late war than ever in the like space before.

senses.d: Having probability; affording probability; probable; likely.
q: But it is like the jolly world about us will scoff at the paradox of these practices.
Many were not easy to be governed, nor like to conform themselves to strict rules.

senses.d: Inclined toward; disposed to; as, to feel like taking a walk.
q: Had like to have been my utter overthrow.
Ramona had like to have said the literal truth, . . . but recollected herself in time.

Like.etym: [OE. lik, ilik, gelic, AS. gelīc, fr. pref. ge- + līc body, and orig. meaning, having the same body, shape, or appearance, and hence, like; akin to OS. gilīk, D. gelijk, G. gleich, OHG. gilīh, Icel. līkr, glīkr, Dan. lig, Sw. lik, Goth. galeiks, OS. lik body, D. lijk, G. leiche, Icel. līk, Sw. lik,

senses.d: That which is equal or similar to another; the counterpart; an exact resemblance; a copy.
q: He was a man, take him for all in all, I shall not look upon his like again.

senses.d: A liking; a preference; inclination; — usually in pl.; as, we all have likes and dislikes.
In a manner like that of; in a manner similar to; as, do not act like him.
q: He maketh them to stagger like a drunken man.

senses.d: In a like or similar manner.
q: Like as a father pitieth his children, so the Lord pitieth them that fear him.

senses.d: Likely; probably.
To suit; to please; to be agreeable to.
q: Cornwall him liked best, therefore he chose there.
I willingly confess that it likes me much better when I find virtue in a fair lodging than when I am bound to seek it in an ill-favored creature.

senses.d: To be pleased with in a moderate degree; to approve; to take satisfaction in; to enjoy.
q: He proceeded from looking to liking, and from liking to loving.

senses.d: To liken; to compare.
q: Like me to the peasant boys of France.

Like.etym: [OE. liken to please, AS. līcian, gelīcian, fr. gelīc. See Like, a.]

senses.d: To be pleased; to choose.
q: He may either go or stay, as he best likes.

senses.d: To have an appearance or expression; to look; to seem to be (in a specified condition).
q: You like well, and bear your years very well.

senses.d: To come near; to avoid with difficulty; to escape narrowly; as, he liked to have been too late. Cf. Had like, under Like, a.
q: He probably got his death, as he liked to have done two years ago, by viewing the troops for the expedition from the wall of Kensington Garden.

senses.d: The stroke which equalizes the number of strokes played by the opposing player or side; as, to play the like.
To allege, or think, to be like; to represent as like; to compare; as, to liken life to a pilgrimage.
q: Whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them, I will liken him unto a wise man which built his house upon a rock.

senses.d: To make or cause to be like.
The state or quality of being like; similitude; resemblance; similarity; as, the likeness of the one to the other is remarkable.
Appearance or form; guise.
q: An enemy in the likeness of a friend.

senses.d: That which closely resembles; a portrait.
q: the likenesses of him which still remain enable us to imagine.

senses.d: A comparison; parable; proverb.
q: He said to them, Soothly ye shall say to me this likeness, Leech, heal thyself.

Likeness.syn: Similarity; parallel; similitude; representation; portrait; effigy.

senses.d: In like manner; also; moreover; too. See Also.
q: Go, and do thou likewise.
For he seeth that wise men die; likewise the fool and the brutish person perish.

senses.d: Looking; appearing; as, better or worse liking. See Like, to look.
q: Why should he see your faces worse liking than the children which are of your sort ?

senses.d: The state of being pleasing; a suiting. See On liking, below.

The state of being pleased with, or attracted toward, some thing or person; hence, inclination; desire; pleasure; preference; — often with for, formerly with to; as, it is an amusement I have no liking for.
q: If the human intellect hath once taken a liking to any doctrine, . . . it draws everything else into harmony with that doctrine, and to its support.

senses.d: Appearance; look; figure; state of body as to health or condition.
q: I shall think the worse of fat men, as long as I have an eye to make difference of men's liking.
Their young ones are in good liking.
Would he be the degenerate scion of that royal line . . . to be a king on liking and on sufferance ?

senses.d: A plant and flower of the genus Lilium, endogenous bulbous plants, having a regular perianth of six colored pieces, six stamens, and a superior three-celled ovary.
A name given to handsome flowering plants of several genera, having some resemblance in color or form to a true lily, as Pancratium, Crinum, Amaryllis, Nerine, etc.
That end of a compass needle which should point to the north; — so called as often ornamented with the figure of a lily or fleur-de-lis.
q: But sailing further, it veers its lily to the west.

Lily.etym: [AS. lilie, L. lilium, Gr. λείριον. Cf. Flower-de-luce.]

senses.d: A royal spade; — usually in pl. See Royal spade, below.
A thong by which a dog is led; a leash.
The linden tree. See Linden.

Lime.etym: [Formerly line, for earlier lind. See Linden.]

senses.d: A fruit allied to the lemon, but much smaller; also, the tree which bears it. There are two kinds; Citrus Medica, var. acida which is intensely sour, and the sweet lime (C. Medica, var. Limetta) which is only slightly sour.

Lime.etym: [F. lime; of Persian origin. See Lemon.]

senses.d: Birdlime.
q: Like the lime That foolish birds are caught with.

senses.d: Oxide of calcium; the white or gray, caustic substance, usually called quicklime, obtained by calcining limestone or shells, the heat driving off carbon dioxide and leaving lime. It develops great heat when treated with water, forming slacked lime, and is an essential ingredient of cement, plastering, mortar, etc.

Lime.etym: [AS. līm; akin to D. lijm, G. leim, OHG. līm, Icel. līm, Sw. lim, Dan. liim, L. limus mud, linere to smear, and E. loam. √126. Cf. Loam, Liniment.]

senses.d: To smear with a viscous substance, as birdlime.
q: These twigs, in time, will come to be limed.

senses.d: To entangle; to insnare.
q: We had limed ourselves With open eyes, and we must take the chance.

senses.d: To treat with lime, or oxide or hydrate of calcium; to manure with lime; as, to lime hides for removing the hair; to lime sails in order to whiten them.
q: Land may be improved by draining, marling, and liming.

senses.d: To cement.

Lime.etym: [Cf. AS. gelīman to glue or join together. See Lime a viscous substance.]

senses.d: That which terminates, circumscribes, restrains, or confines; the bound, border, or edge; the utmost extent; as, the limit of a walk, of a town, of a country; the limits of human knowledge or endeavor.
q: As eager of the chase, the maid Beyond the forest's verdant limits strayed.

senses.d: The space or thing defined by limits.
q: The archdeacon hath divided it Into three limits very equally.

senses.d: That which terminates a period of time; hence, the period itself; the full time or extent.
q: The dateless limit of thy dear exile.
The limit of your lives is out.

senses.d: A restriction; a check; a curb; a hindrance.
q: I prithee, give no limits to my tongue.

senses.d: A determining feature; a distinguishing characteristic; a differentia.

A determinate quantity, to which a variable one continually approaches, and may differ from it by less than any given difference, but to which, under the law of variation, the variable can never become exactly equivalent.

Limit.syn: Boundary; border; edge; termination; restriction; bound; confine.
Limit.etym: [From L. limes, limitis: cf. F. limite; or from E. limit, v. See Limit, v. t.]

senses.d: To apply a limit to, or set a limit for; to terminate, circumscribe, or restrict, by a limit or limits; as, to limit the acreage of a crop; to limit the issue of paper money; to limit one's ambitions or aspirations; to limit the meaning of a word.

Limit.etym: [F. limiter, L. limitare, fr. limes, limitis, limit; prob. akin to limen threshold, E. eliminate; cf. L. limus sidelong.]

senses.d: To beg, or to exercise functions, within a certain limited region; as, a limiting friar.
Confined within limits; narrow; circumscribed; restricted; as, our views of nature are very limited.
To yield; to stop; to cease.
To cease from.
A pool or collection of water, particularly one above or below a fall of water.
A waterfall, or cataract; as, a roaring lin.
A steep ravine.

Lin.etym: [Ir. linn, or Gael. linne; akin to W. llyn a pool, pond, lake, but in senses 2 and 3 prob. from AS. hlynn torrent. Cf. Dunlin.]

senses.d: Flax; linen.
The longer and finer fiber of flax.
To cover the inner surface of; as, to line a cloak with silk or fur; to line a box with paper or tin.
q: The inside lined with rich carnation silk.

senses.d: To put something in the inside of; to fill; to supply, as a purse with money.
q: The charge amounteth very high for any one man's purse, except lined beyond ordinary, to reach unto.
Till coffee has her stomach lined.

senses.d: To place persons or things along the side of for security or defense; to strengthen by adding anything; to fortify; as, to line works with soldiers.
q: Line and new repair our towns of war With men of courage and with means defendant.

senses.d: To impregnate; — applied to brute animals.
A linen thread or string; a slender, strong cord; also, a cord of any thickness; a rope; a hawser; as, a fishing line; a line for snaring birds; a clothesline; a towline.
q: Who so layeth lines for to latch fowls.

senses.d: A more or less threadlike mark of pen, pencil, or graver; any long mark; as, a chalk line.
The course followed by anything in motion; hence, a road or route; as, the arrow descended in a curved line; the place is remote from lines of travel.
Direction; as, the line of sight or vision.
A row of letters, words, etc., written or printed; esp., a row of words extending across a page or column.
A short letter; a note; as, a line from a friend.
A verse, or the words which form a certain number of feet, according to the measure.
q: In the preceding line Ulysses speaks of Nausicaa.

senses.d: Course of conduct, thought, occupation, or policy; method of argument; department of industry, trade, or intellectual activity.
q: He is uncommonly powerful in his own line, but it is not the line of a first-rate man.

senses.d: That which has length, but not breadth or thickness.
The exterior limit of a figure, plat, or territory; boundary; contour; outline.
q: Eden stretched her line From Auran eastward to the royal towers Of great Seleucia.

senses.d: A threadlike crease marking the face or the hand; hence, characteristic mark.
q: Though on his brow were graven lines austere.
He tipples palmistry, and dines On all her fortune-telling lines.

senses.d: Lineament; feature; figure.

Line.etym: [OE. line, AS. līne cable, hawser, prob. from L. linea a linen thread, string, line, fr. linum flax, thread, linen, cable; but the English word was influenced by F. ligne line, from the same L. word linea. See Linen.]

senses.d: To mark with a line or lines; to cover with lines; as, to line a copy book.
q: He had a healthy color in his cheeks, and his face, though lined, bore few traces of anxiety.

senses.d: To represent by lines; to delineate; to portray.
To read or repeat line by line; as, to line out a hymn.
q: This custom of reading or lining, or, as it was frequently called, “deaconing” the hymn or psalm in the churches, was brought about partly from necessity.

senses.d: To form into a line; to align; as, to line troops.
Descent in a line from a common progenitor; progeny; race; descending line of offspring or ascending line of parentage.
q: Both the lineage and the certain sire From which I sprung, from me are hidden yet.

Lineage.etym: [OE. linage, F. lignage, fr. L. linea line. See 3d Line.]

senses.d: Made of linen; as, linen cloth; a linen stocking.
Resembling linen cloth; white; pale.

Linen.etym: [OE., fr. lin linen. See Linen, n.]

senses.d: Thread or cloth made of flax or (rarely) of hemp; — used in a general sense to include cambric, shirting, sheeting, towels, tablecloths, etc.
Underclothing, esp. the shirt, as being, in former times, chiefly made of linen.

Linen.etym: [Prop. an adj. from OE. lin flax, AS. līn flax, whence līnen made of flax; akin to OS., Icel., & MHG. līn flax and linen, G. lein, leinen, linen, Sw. lin flax, Goth. lein linen, L. linum flax, linen, Gr. λίνον. Cf. Line, Linseed.]

senses.d: To delay; to loiter; to remain or wait long; to be slow or reluctant in parting or moving; to be slow in deciding; to be in suspense; to hesitate.
q: Nor cast one longing, lingering look behind.
Perhaps thou linger'st, in deep thoughts detained.

Linger.syn: To loiter; lag; saunter; delay; tarry; stop; hesitate.
Linger.etym: [OE. lengen to tarry, AS. lengan to prolong, put off, fr. lang long. √125. See Long, a.]

senses.d: To protract; to draw out.
q: She lingers my desires.

senses.d: To spend or pass in a lingering manner; — with out; as, to linger out one's days on a sick bed.
A horizontal member spanning an opening, and carrying the superincumbent weight by means of its strength in resisting crosswise fracture.

Lintel.etym: [OF. lintel, F. linteau, LL. lintellus, for limitellus, a dim. fr. L. limes limit. See Limit.]

senses.d: A large carnivorous feline mammal (Felis leo), found in Southern Asia and in most parts of Africa, distinct varieties occurring in the different countries. The adult male, in most varieties, has a thick mane of long shaggy hair that adds to his apparent size, which is less than that of the largest tigers. The length, however, is sometimes eleven feet to the base of the tail. The color is a tawny yellow or yellowish brown; the mane is darker, and the terminal tuft of the tail is black. In one variety, called the maneless lion, the male has only a slight mane.
A sign and a constellation; Leo.
An object of interest and curiosity, especially a person who is so regarded; as, he was quite a lion in London at that time.
q: Such society was far more enjoyable than that of Edinburgh, for here he was not a lion, but a man.

Lion.etym: [F. lion, L. leo, -onis, akin to Gr. λέων. Cf. Chameleon, Dandelion, Leopard.]

senses.d: A female lion.
Like a lion; brave as a lion.

One of the two fleshy folds which surround the orifice of the mouth in man and many other animals. In man the lips are organs of speech essential to certain articulations. Hence, by a figure they denote the mouth, or all the organs of speech, and sometimes speech itself.
q: Thine own lips testify against thee.

senses.d: An edge of an opening; a thin projecting part of anything; a kind of short open spout; as, the lip of a vessel.
The sharp cutting edge on the end of an auger.
One of the two opposite divisions of a labiate corolla.
One of the edges of the aperture of a univalve shell.

Lip.etym: [OE. lippe, AS. lippa; akin to D. lip, G. lippe, lefze, OHG. lefs, Dan. læbe, Sw. läpp, L. labium, labrum. Cf. Labial.]

senses.d: To touch with the lips; to put the lips to; hence, to kiss.
q: The bubble on the wine which breaks Before you lip the glass.
A hand that kings Have lipped and trembled kissing.

senses.d: To utter; to speak.
To clip; to trim.
Any liquid substance, as water, milk, blood, sap, juice, or the like.
Specifically, alcoholic or spirituous fluid, either distilled or fermented, as brandy, wine, whisky, beer, etc.
A solution of a medicinal substance in water; — distinguished from tincture and aqua.

Liquor.etym: [OE. licour, licur, OF. licur, F. liqueur, fr. L. liquor, fr. liquere to be liquid. See Liquid, and cf. Liqueur.]

senses.d: To supply with liquor.
To grease.
q: Liquor fishermen's boots.

senses.d: A line inclosing or forming the extremity of a piece of ground, or field of combat; hence, in the plural (lists), the ground or field inclosed for a race or combat.
q: In measured lists to toss the weighty lance.

List.etym: [F. lice, LL. liciae, pl., from L. licium thread, girdle.]

senses.d: To inclose for combat; as, to list a field.
To hearken; to attend; to listen.
q: Stand close, and list to him.

senses.d: To listen or hearken to.
q: Then weigh what loss your honor may sustain, If with too credent ear you list his songs.

senses.d: To desire or choose; to please.
q: The wind bloweth where it listeth.
Them that add to the Word of God what them listeth.
Let other men think of your devices as they list.

senses.d: To lean; to incline; as, the ship lists to port.

List.etym: [OE. listen, lusten, AS. lystan, from lust pleasure. See Lust.]

senses.d: Inclination; desire.
An inclination to one side; as, the ship has a list to starboard.
A strip forming the woven border or selvedge of cloth, particularly of broadcloth, and serving to strengthen it; hence, a strip of cloth; a fillet.
A limit or boundary; a border.
q: The very list, the very utmost bound, Of all our fortunes.

senses.d: The lobe of the ear; the ear itself.
A stripe.
A roll or catalogue, that is, a row or line; a record of names; as, a list of names, books, articles; a list of ratable estate.
q: He was the ablest emperor of all the list.

senses.d: A little square molding; a fillet; — called also listel.
A narrow strip of wood, esp. sapwood, cut from the edge of a plank or board.
A piece of woolen cloth with which the yarns are grasped by a workman.
The first thin coat of tin.

List.etym: [AS. līst a list of cloth; akin to D. lijst, G. leiste, OHG. līsta, Icel. lista, listi, Sw. list, Dan. liste. In sense 5 from F. liste, of German origin, and thus ultimately the same word.]

senses.d: To sew together, as strips of cloth, so as to make a show of colors, or form a border.
To cover with list, or with strips of cloth; to put list on; as, to list a door; to stripe as if with list.
q: The tree that stood white-listed through the gloom.

senses.d: To enroll; to place or register in a list.
q: Listed among the upper serving men.

senses.d: To engage, as a soldier; to enlist.
q: I will list you for my soldier.

senses.d: To cut away a narrow strip, as of sapwood, from the edge of; as, to list a board.
To engage in public service by enrolling one's name; to enlist.
To plow and plant with a lister.
In cotton culture, to prepare, as land, for the crop by making alternating beds and alleys with the hoe.
To give close attention with the purpose of hearing; to give ear; to hearken; to attend.
q: When we have occasion to listen, and give a more particular attention to some sound, the tympanum is drawn to a more than ordinary tension.

senses.d: To give heed; to yield to advice; to follow admonition; to obey.
q: Listen to me, and by me be ruled.
Soldiers note forts, armories, and magazines; scholars listen after libraries, disputations, and professors.

Listen.etym: [OE. listnen, listen, lustnen, lusten, AS. hlystan; akin to hlyst hearing, OS. hlust, Icel. hlusta to listen, hlust ear, AS. hlosnian to wait in suspense, OHG. hlosēn to listen, Gr. κλύειν, and E. loud. √41. See Loud, and cf. List to listen.]

senses.d: To attend to.
A bed or stretcher so arranged that a person, esp. a sick or wounded person, may be easily carried in or upon it.
q: There is a litter ready; lay him in 't.

senses.d: Straw, hay, etc., scattered on a floor, as bedding for animals to rest on; also, a covering of straw for plants.
q: To crouch in litter of your stable planks.
Take off the litter from your kernel beds.

senses.d: Things lying scattered about in a manner indicating slovenliness; scattered rubbish.
q: Strephon, who found the room was void. Stole in, and took a strict survey Of all the litter as it lay.

senses.d: Disorder or untidiness resulting from scattered rubbish, or from thongs lying about uncared for; as, a room in a state of litter.
The young brought forth at one time, by a sow or other multiparous animal, taken collectively. Also Fig.
q: A wolf came to a sow, and very kindly offered to take care of her litter.
Reflect upon that numerous litter of strange, senseless opinions that crawl about the world.

Litter.etym: [F. litière, LL. lectaria, fr. L. lectus couch, bed. See Lie to be prostrated, and cf. Coverlet.]

senses.d: To supply with litter, as cattle; to cover with litter, as the floor of a stall.
q: Tell them how they litter their jades.
For his ease, well littered was the floor.

senses.d: To put into a confused or disordered condition; to strew with scattered articles; as, to litter a room.
q: The room with volumes littered round.

senses.d: To give birth to; to bear; — said of brutes, esp. those which produce more than one at a birth, and also of human beings, in abhorrence or contempt.
q: We might conceive that dogs were created blind, because we observe they were littered so with us.
The son that she did litter here, A freckled whelp hagborn.

senses.d: To be supplied with litter as bedding; to sleep or make one's bed in litter.
q: The inn Where he and his horse littered.

senses.d: To produce a litter.
q: A desert . . . where the she-wolf still littered.

senses.d: Small in size or extent; not big; diminutive; — opposed to big or large; as, a little body; a little animal; a little piece of ground; a little hill; a little distance; a little child.
q: He sought to see Jesus who he was; and could not for the press, because he was little of stature.

senses.d: Short in duration; brief; as, a little sleep.
q: Best him enough: after a little time, I'll beat him too.

senses.d: Small in quantity or amount; not much; as, a little food; a little air or water.
q: Conceited of their little wisdoms, and doting upon their own fancies.

senses.d: Small in dignity, power, or importance; not great; insignificant; contemptible.
q: When thou wast little in thine own sight, wast thou not made the head of the tribes?

senses.d: Small in force or efficiency; not strong; weak; slight; inconsiderable; as, little attention or exertion;little effort; little care or diligence.
q: By sad experiment I know How little weight my words with thee can find.

senses.d: Small in extent of views or sympathies; narrow; shallow; contracted; mean; illiberal; ungenerous.
q: The long-necked geese of the world that are ever hissing dispraise, Because their natures are little.
The men, and the women, and the little ones.

Little.etym: [OE. litel, lutel, AS. l�tel, lītel, l�t; akin to OS. littil, D. luttel, LG. lütt, OHG. luzzil, MHG. lützel; and perh. to AS. lytig deceitful, lot deceit, Goth. liuts deceitful, lut�n to deceive; cf. also Icel. lītill little, Sw. liten, Dan. liden, lille, Goth. leitils, which appear to have a differ

senses.d: That which is little; a small quantity, amount, space, or the like.
q: Much was in little writ.
There are many expressions, which carrying with them no clear ideas, are like to remove but little of my ignorance.

senses.d: A small degree or scale; miniature.
q: A little, to or in a small degree; to a limited extent; somewhat; for a short time. “ Stay a little.”
The painter flattered her a little.

senses.d: by slow degrees; piecemeal; gradually.
In a small quantity or degree; not much; slightly; somewhat; — often with a preceding it.
an Englishman opposed to territorial expansion of the British Empire. See Antiimperialism, above.
the quahog, or round clam.
a disease of peaches in which the fruit is much dwarfed, and the leaves grow small and thin. The cause is not known.
Rhode Island; — a nickname alluding to its small size. It is the smallest State of the United States.
an order of women who care for old men and women and infirm poor, for whom special houses are built. It was established at St. Servan, Britany, France, in 1840, by the Abbé Le Pailleur.
the winning of 12 out of the 13 tricks. It counts 20 points on the honor score.

To be alive; to have life; to have, as an animal or a plant, the capacity of assimilating matter as food, and to be dependent on such assimilation for a continuance of existence; as, animals and plants that live to a great age are long in reaching maturity.
q: Thus saith the Lord God unto these bones; Behold, I will . . . lay sinews upon you, and will bring up flesh upon you, and cover you with skin, and put breath in you, and ye shall live.

senses.d: To pass one's time; to pass life or time in a certain manner, as to habits, conduct, or circumstances; as, to live in ease or affluence; to live happily or usefully.
q: O death, how bitter is the remembrance of thee to a man that liveth at rest in his possessions!

senses.d: To make one's abiding place or home; to abide; to dwell; to reside.
q: Jacob lived in the land of Egypt seventeen years.

senses.d: To be or continue in existence; to exist; to remain; to be permanent; to last; — said of inanimate objects, ideas, etc.
q: Men's evil manners live in brass; their virtues We write in water.

senses.d: To enjoy or make the most of life; to be in a state of happiness.
q: What greater curse could envious fortune give Than just to die when I began to live?

senses.d: To feed; to subsist; to be nourished or supported; — with on; as, horses live on grass and grain.
To have a spiritual existence; to be quickened, nourished, and actuated by divine influence or faith.
q: The just shall live by faith.

senses.d: To be maintained in life; to acquire a livelihood; to subsist; — with on or by; as, to live on spoils.
q: Those who live by labor.

senses.d: To outlast danger; to float; — said of a ship, boat, etc.; as, no ship could live in such a storm.
q: A strong mast that lived upon the sea.

Live.etym: [OE. liven, livien, AS. libban, lifian; akin to OS. libbian, D. leven, G. leben, OHG. lebēn, Dan. leve, Sw. lefva, Icel. lifa to live, to be left, to remain, Goth. liban to live; akin to E. leave to forsake, and life, Gr. λιπαρει̑ν to persist, λιπαρόσ oily, shining, sleek, λίποσ fat, lard, Skr. lip

senses.d: To spend, as one's life; to pass; to maintain; to continue in, constantly or habitually; as, to live an idle or a useful life.
To act habitually in conformity with; to practice.
q: To live the Gospel.

senses.d: Having life; alive; living; not dead.
q: If one man's ox hurt another's, that he die; then they shall sell the live ox, and divide the money of it.

senses.d: Being in a state of ignition; burning; having active properties; as, a live coal; live embers.
Full of earnestness; active; wide awake; glowing; as, a live man, or orator.
Vivid; bright.
Imparting power; having motion; as, the live spindle of a lathe.
Life.
Having life; — used only in composition; as, long-lived; short-lived.
Endowed with or manifesting life; living.
q: Chaplets of gold and silver resembling lively flowers and leaves.

senses.d: Brisk; vivacious; active; as, a lively youth.
q: But wherefore comes old Manoa in such haste, With youthful steps ? Much livelier than erewhile He seems.

senses.d: Gay; airy; animated; spirited.
q: From grave to gay, from lively to severe.

senses.d: Representing life; lifelike.
q: I spied the lively picture of my father.

senses.d: Bright; vivid; glowing; strong; vigorous.
q: The colors of the prism are manifestly more full, intense, and lively that those of natural bodies.
His faith must be not only living, but lively too.

Lively.syn: Brisk; vigorous; quick; nimble; smart; active; alert; sprightly; animated; spirited; prompt; earnest; strong; energetic; vivid; vivacious; blithe; gleeful; airy; gay; jocund.

senses.d: In a brisk, active, or animated manner; briskly; vigorously.
With strong resemblance of life.
q: Thou counterfeitest most lively.

senses.d: One who, or that which, lives.
q: And try if life be worth the liver's care.

senses.d: A resident; a dweller; as, a liver in Brooklyn.
One whose course of life has some marked characteristic (expressed by an adjective); as, a free liver.
A very large glandular and vascular organ in the visceral cavity of all vertebrates.

Liver.etym: [AS. lifer; akin to D. liver, G. leber, OHG. lebara, Icel. lifr, Sw. lefver, and perh. to Gr. � fat, E. live, v.]

senses.d: The glossy ibis (Ibis falcinellus); — said to have given its name to the city of Liverpool.
Alive; living; with life.
Being alive; having life; as, a living creature.
Active; lively; vigorous; — said esp. of states of the mind, and sometimes of abstract things; as, a living faith; a living principle.
Issuing continually from the earth; running; flowing; as, a living spring; — opposed to stagnant.
Producing life, action, animation, or vigor; quickening.
Ignited; glowing with heat; burning; live.
q: Then on the living coals wine they pour.

senses.d: The state of one who, or that which, lives; lives; life; existence.
Manner of life; as, riotous living; penurious living; earnest living.
Means of subsistence; sustenance; estate.
q: She can spin for her living.
He divided unto them his living.

senses.d: Power of continuing life; the act of living, or living comfortably.
q: There is no living without trusting somebody or other in some cases.

senses.d: The benefice of a clergyman; an ecclesiastical charge which a minister receives.
q: He could not get a deanery, a prebend, or even a living

senses.d: Any one of the numerous species of reptiles belonging to the order Lacertilia; sometimes, also applied to reptiles of other orders, as the Hatteria.
A piece of rope with thimble or block spliced into one or both of the ends.
A piece of timber with a forked end, used in dragging a heavy stone, a log, or the like, from a field.

Lizard.etym: [OE. lesarde, OF. lesarde, F. lézard, L. lacerta, lacertus. Cf. Alligator, Lacerta.]

senses.d: Look; see; behold; observe.

Lo.etym: [OE. lo, low; perh. akin to E. look, v.]

senses.d: A burden; that which is laid on or put in anything for conveyance; that which is borne or sustained; a weight; as, a heavy load.
q: He might such a load To town with his ass carry.

senses.d: The quantity which can be carried or drawn in some specified way; the contents of a cart, barrow, or vessel; that which will constitute a cargo; lading.
That which burdens, oppresses, or grieves the mind or spirits; as, a load of care.

A particular measure for certain articles, being as much as may be carried at one time by the conveyance commonly used for the article measured; as, a load of wood; a load of hay; specifically, five quarters.
The charge of a firearm; as, a load of powder.
Weight or violence of blows.
The work done by a steam engine or other prime mover when working.

Load.syn: Burden; lading; weight; cargo. See Burden.
Load.etym: [OE. lode load, way; properly the same word as lode, but confused with lade, load, v. See Lade, Lead, v., Lode.]

senses.d: To lay a load or burden on or in, as on a horse or in a cart; to charge with a load, as a gun; to furnish with a lading or cargo, as a ship; hence, to add weight to, so as to oppress or embarrass; to heap upon.
q: I strive all in vain to load the cart.
I have loaden me with many spoils.
Those honors deep and broad, wherewith Your majesty loads our house.

senses.d: To adulterate or drug; as, to load wine.
To magnetize.
Any thick lump, mass, or cake; especially, a large regularly shaped or molded mass, as of bread, sugar, or cake.

Loaf.etym: [OE. lof, laf, AS. hlāf; akin to G. laib, OHG. hleip, Icel. hleifr, Goth. hlaifs, Russ. khlieb', Lith. klëpas. Cf. Lady, Lammas, Lord.]

senses.d: To spend time in idleness; to lounge or loiter about.

Loaf.etym: [G. laufen to run, Prov. G. loofen. See Leap.]

senses.d: To spend in idleness; — with away; as, to loaf time away.
A loanin.
The act of lending; a lending; permission to use; as, the loan of a book, money, services.
That which one lends or borrows, esp. a sum of money lent at interest; as, he repaid the loan.

Loan.etym: [OE. lone, lane, AS. lān, læn, fr. león to lend; akin to D. leen loan, fief, G. lehen fief, Icel. lān, G. leihen to lend, OHG. līhan, Icel. ljī, Goth. leihwan, L. linquere to leave, Gr. λείπειν, Skr. ric. √119. Cf. Delinquent, Eclipse, Eleven, Ellipse, Lend, License, Relic.]

senses.d: To lend; — sometimes with out.
q: By way of location or loaning them out.

senses.d: Hateful; odious; disliked.
Filled with disgust or aversion; averse; unwilling; reluctant; as, loath to part.
q: Full loth were him to curse for his tithes.
Why, then, though loath, yet must I be content.

Loath.etym: [OE. looth, loth, AS. lāð hostile, odious; akin to OS. lāð, G. leid, Icel. leiðr, Sw. led, G. leiden to suffer, OHG. līdan to suffer, go, cf. AS. līðan to go, Goth. leipan, and E. lead to guide.]

senses.d: To feel extreme disgust at, or aversion for.
q: Loathing the honeyed cakes, I Ionged for bread.

senses.d: To dislike greatly; to abhor; to hate.
q: The secret which I loathe.
She loathes the vital sir.

Loathe.syn: To hate; abhor; detest; abominate. See Hate.

senses.d: To feel disgust or nausea.
Fitted to cause loathing; exciting disgust; disgusting.
q: The most loathsome and deadly forms of infection.

senses.d: A tuft of hair; a flock or small quantity of wool, hay, or other like substance; a tress or ringlet of hair.
q: These gray locks, the pursuivants of death.

Lock.etym: [AS. locc; akin to D. lok, G. locke, OHG. loc, Icel. lokkr, and perh. to Gr. � to bend, twist.]

senses.d: Anything that fastens; specifically, a fastening, as for a door, a lid, a trunk, a drawer, and the like, in which a bolt is moved by a key so as to hold or to release the thing fastened.
A fastening together or interlacing; a closing of one thing upon another; a state of being fixed or immovable.
q: Albemarle Street closed by a lock of carriages.

senses.d: A place from which egress is prevented, as by a lock.
The barrier or works which confine the water of a stream or canal.
An inclosure in a canal with gates at each end, used in raising or lowering boats as they pass from one level to another; — called also lift lock.
That part or apparatus of a firearm by which the charge is exploded; as, a matchlock, flintlock, percussion lock, etc.
A device for keeping a wheel from turning.
A grapple in wrestling.

Lock.etym: [AS. loc inclosure, an inclosed place, the fastening of a door, fr. lūcan to lock, fasten; akin to OS. lūkan (in comp.), D. luiken, OHG. lūhhan, Icel. l�ka, Goth. lūkan (in comp.); cf. Skr. ruj to break. Cf. Locket.]

senses.d: To fasten with a lock, or as with a lock; to make fast; to prevent free movement of; as, to lock a door, a carriage wheel, a river, etc.
To prevent ingress or access to, or exit from, by fastening the lock or locks of; — often with up; as, to lock or lock up, a house, jail, room, trunk. etc.

To fasten in or out, or to make secure by means of, or as with, locks; to confine, or to shut in or out — often with up; as, to lock one's self in a room; to lock up the prisoners; to lock up one's silver; to lock intruders out of the house; to lock money into a vault; to lock a child in one's arms; to lock a secret in one's breast.
To link together; to clasp closely; as, to lock arms.
To furnish with locks; also, to raise or lower (a boat) in a lock.
To seize, as the sword arm of an antagonist, by turning the left arm around it, to disarm him.
To become fast, as by means of a lock or by interlacing; as, the door locks close.
q: When it locked none might through it pass.

senses.d: Any one of numerous species of long-winged, migratory, orthopterous insects, of the family Acrididæ, allied to the grasshoppers; esp., (Edipoda, or Pachytylus, migratoria, and Acridium perigrinum, of Southern Europe, Asia, and Africa. In the United States the related species with similar habits are usually called grasshoppers. See Grasshopper.
The locust tree. See Locust Tree (definition, note, and phrases).
A shelter in which one may rest;
q: Their lodges and their tentis up they gan bigge .
O for a lodge in some vast wilderness!

senses.d: A small dwelling house, as for a gamekeeper or gatekeeper of an estate.
A den or cave.
The meeting room of an association; hence, the regularly constituted body of members which meets there; as, a masonic lodge.
The chamber of an abbot, prior, or head of a college.
The space at the mouth of a level next the shaft, widened to permit wagons to pass, or ore to be deposited for hoisting; — called also platt.
A collection of objects lodged together.
q: The Maldives, a famous lodge of islands.

senses.d: A family of North American Indians, or the persons who usually occupy an Indian lodge, — as a unit of enumeration, reckoned from four to six persons; as, the tribe consists of about two hundred lodges, that is, of about a thousand individuals.

Lodge.etym: [OE. loge, logge, F. loge, LL. laubia porch, gallery, fr. OHG. louba, G. laube, arbor, bower, fr. lab foliage. See Leaf, and cf. Lobby, Loggia.]

senses.d: To rest or remain a lodge house, or other shelter; to rest; to stay; to abide; esp., to sleep at night; as, to lodge in York Street.
q: Stay and lodge by me this night.
Something holy lodges in that breast.

senses.d: To fall or lie down, as grass or grain, when overgrown or beaten down by the wind.
To come to a rest; to stop and remain; as, the bullet lodged in the bark of a tree.
To give shelter or rest to; especially, to furnish a sleeping place for; to harbor; to shelter; hence, to receive; to hold.
q: Every house was proud to lodge a knight.
The memory can lodge a greater store of images than all the senses can present at one time.

senses.d: To drive to shelter; to track to covert.
q: The deer is lodged; I have tracked her to her covert.

senses.d: To deposit for keeping or preservation; as, the men lodged their arms in the arsenal.
To cause to stop or rest in; to implant.
q: He lodged an arrow in a tender breast.

senses.d: To lay down; to prostrate.
q: Though bladed corn be lodged, and trees blown down.

Lodge.etym: [OE. loggen, OF. logier, F. loger. See Lodge, n. ]

senses.d: Lying down; — used of beasts of the chase, as couchant is of beasts of prey.
The act of one who, or that which, lodges.
A place of rest, or of temporary habitation; esp., a sleeping apartment; — often in the plural with a singular meaning.
q: Wits take lodgings in the sound of Bow.

senses.d: Abiding place; harbor; cover.
q: Fair bosom . . . the lodging of delight.

senses.d: That which is lifted up; an elevation.
The room or space under a roof and above the ceiling of the uppermost story.
A gallery or raised apartment in a church, hall, etc.; as, an organ loft.
A floor or room placed above another; a story.
q: Eutychus . . . fell down from the third loft.

Loft.etym: [Icel. lopt air, heaven, loft, upper room; akin to AS. lyft air, G. luft, Dan. loft loft, Goth. luftus air. Cf. Lift, v. & n. ]

senses.d: Lofty; proud.
Pitch or slope of the face of a club (tending to drive the ball upward).
To make or furnish with a loft; to cause to have loft; as, a lofted house; a lofted golf-club head.
q: A wooden club with a lofted face.

senses.d: To raise aloft; to send into the air;
to strike (the ball) so that it will go over an obstacle.
In a lofty manner or position; haughtily.
The state or quality of being lofty.
Lifted high up; having great height; towering; high.
q: See lofty Lebanon his head advance.

senses.d: Fig.: Elevated in character, rank, dignity, spirit, bearing, language, etc.; exalted; noble; stately; characterized by pride; haughty.
q: The high and lofty One, that inhabiteth eternity.
Lofty and sour to them that loved him not
Himself to sing, and build the lofty rhyme.

Lofty.syn: Tall; high; exalted; dignified; stately; majestic; sublime; proud; haughty. See Tall.

senses.d: A Hebrew measure of liquids, containing 2.37 gills.
A bulky piece of wood which has not been shaped by hewing or sawing.
An apparatus for measuring the rate of a ship's motion through the water.
Hence: The record of the rate of ship's speed or of her daily progress; also, the full nautical record of a ship's cruise or voyage; a log slate; a log book.
A record and tabulated statement of the work done by an engine, as of a steamship, of the coal consumed, and of other items relating to the performance of machinery during a given time.
A weight or block near the free end of a hoisting rope to prevent it from being drawn through the sheave.

Log.etym: [Icel. lāg a felled tree, log; akin to E. lie. See Lie to lie prostrate.]

senses.d: To enter in a ship's log book; as, to log the miles run.
To engage in the business of cutting or transporting logs for timber; to get out logs.
To move to and fro; to rock.

That part of a human being or quadruped, which extends on either side of the spinal column between the hip bone and the false ribs. In human beings the loins are also called the reins. See Illust. of Beef.

Loin.etym: [OE. loine, OF. logne, F. longe, from (assumed) LL. lumbea, L. lumbus join. Cf. Lends, Lumbar, Nombles.]

senses.d: Drawn out in a line, or in the direction of length; protracted; extended; as, a long line; — opposed to short, and distinguished from broad or wide.
Drawn out or extended in time; continued through a considerable tine, or to a great length; as, a long series of events; a long debate; a long drama; a long history; a long book.
Slow in passing; causing weariness by length or duration; lingering; as, long hours of watching.
Occurring or coming after an extended interval; distant in time; far away.
q: The we may us reserve both fresh and strong Against the tournament, which is not long.

senses.d: Extended to any specified measure; of a specified length; as, a span long; a yard long; a mile long, that is, extended to the measure of a mile, etc.
Far-reaching; extensive.
Prolonged, or relatively more prolonged, in utterance; — said of vowels and syllables. See Short, a., 13, and Guide to Pronunciation, §§ 22, 30.

Long.etym: [AS. long, lang; akin to OS, OFries., D., & G. lang, Icel. langr, Sw. lång, Dan. lang, Goth. laggs, L. longus. √125. Cf. Length, Ling a fish, Linger, Lunge, Purloin.]

senses.d: A note formerly used in music, one half the length of a large, twice that of a breve.
A long sound, syllable, or vowel.
The longest dimension; the greatest extent; — in the phrase, the long and the short of it, that is, the sum and substance of it.
To a great extent in space; as, a long drawn out line.
To a great extent in time; during a long time.
q: They that tarry long at the wine.
When the trumpet soundeth long.

senses.d: At a point of duration far distant, either prior or posterior; as, not long before; not long after; long before the foundation of Rome; long after the Conquest.
Through the whole extent or duration.
q: The bird of dawning singeth all night long.

senses.d: Through an extent of time, more or less; — only in question; as, how long will you be gone?
By means of; by the fault of; because of.
To feel a strong or morbid desire or craving; to wish for something with eagerness; — followed by an infinitive, or by after or for.
q: I long to see you.
I have longed after thy precepts.
I have longed for thy salvation.
Nicomedes, longing for herrings, was supplied with fresh ones . . . at a great distance from the sea.

senses.d: To belong; — used with to, unto, or for.
q: The labor which that longeth unto me.

Long.etym: [AS. langian to increase, to lengthen, to stretch out the mind after, to long, to crave, to belong to, fr. lang long. See Long, a.]

senses.d: Having a supply of stocks or goods; prepared for, or depending for a profit upon, advance in prices; as, long of cotton. Hence, the phrases: to be, or go, long of the market, to be on the long side of the market, to hold products or securities for a rise in price, esp. when bought on a margin.
A thrust. See Lunge.
The training ground for a horse.
Same as 4th Lunge.
One who longs for anything.
An eager desire; a craving; a morbid appetite; an earnest wish; an aspiration.
q: Put on my crown; I have immortal longings in me.

senses.d: To direct the eyes for the purpose of seeing something; to direct the eyes toward an object; to observe with the eyes while keeping them directed; — with various prepositions, often in a special or figurative sense. See Phrases below.
To direct the attention (to something); to consider; to examine; as, to look at an action.
To seem; to appear; to have a particular appearance; as, the patient looks better; the clouds look rainy.
q: It would look more like vanity than gratitude.
Observe how such a practice looks in another person.

senses.d: To have a particular direction or situation; to face; to front.
q: The inner gate that looketh to north.
The east gate . . . which looketh eastward.

senses.d: In the imperative: see; behold; take notice; take care; observe; — used to call attention.
q: Look, how much we thus expel of sin, so much we expel of virtue.
Look that ye bind them fast.
Look if it be my daughter.

senses.d: To show one's self in looking, as by leaning out of a window; as, look out of the window while I speak to you. Sometimes used figuratively.
q: My toes look through the overleather.

senses.d: To await the appearance of anything; to expect; to anticipate.
q: Looking each hour into death's mouth to fall.

Look.etym: [OE. loken, AS. lōcian; akin to G. lugen, OHG. luogēn.]

senses.d: To look at; to turn the eyes toward.
To seek; to search for.
q: Looking my love, I go from place to place.

senses.d: To expect.
To influence, overawe, or subdue by looks or presence as, to look down opposition.
q: A spirit fit to start into an empire, And look the world to law.

senses.d: To express or manifest by a look.
q: Soft eyes looked love to eyes which spake again.

senses.d: The act of looking; a glance; a sight; a view; — often in certain phrases; as, to have, get, take, throw, or cast, a look.
q: Threw many a northward look to see his father Bring up his powers; but he did long in vain.

senses.d: Expression of the eyes and face; manner; as, a proud or defiant look.
q: Up ! up! my friends, and clear your looks.

senses.d: Hence; Appearance; aspect; as, the house has a gloomy look; the affair has a bad look.
q: Pain, disgrace, and poverty have frighted looks.
There was something that reminded me of Dante's Hell in the look of this.

senses.d: Having a certain look or appearance; — often compounded with adjectives; as, good-looking, grand-looking, etc.
The act of one who looks; a glance.
The manner in which one looks; appearance; countenance; face.
q: All dreary was his cheer and his looking.

senses.d: A mass of iron in a pasty condition gathered into a ball for the tilt hammer or rolls.

Loop.etym: [G. luppe an iron lump. Cf. Looping.]

senses.d: A fold or doubling of a thread, cord, rope, etc., through which another thread, cord, etc., can be passed, or which a hook can be hooked into; an eye, as of metal; a staple; a noose; a bight.
q: That the probation bear no hinge, nor loop To hang a doubt on.

senses.d: A small, narrow opening; a loophole.
q: And stop all sight-holes, every loop from whence The eye of Reason may pry in upon us.

senses.d: A curve of any kind in the form of a loop.
A wire forming part of a main circuit and returning to the point from which it starts.
The portion of a vibrating string, air column, etc., between two nodes; — called also ventral segment.

Loop.etym: [Cf. Ir. & Gael. lub loop, noose, fold, thong, bend, lub to bend, incline.]

senses.d: To make a loop of or in; to fasten with a loop or loops; — often with up; as, to loop a string; to loop up a curtain.
Praise; fame; reputation.
q: Good conscience and good loos.

senses.d: Unbound; untied; unsewed; not attached, fastened, fixed, or confined; as, the loose sheets of a book.
q: Her hair, nor loose, nor tied in formal plat.

senses.d: Free from constraint or obligation; not bound by duty, habit, etc.; — with from or of.
q: Now I stand Loose of my vow; but who knows Cato's thoughts ?

senses.d: Not tight or close; as, a loose garment.
Not dense, close, compact, or crowded; as, a cloth of loose texture.
q: With horse and chariots ranked in loose array.

senses.d: Not precise or exact; vague; indeterminate; as, a loose style, or way of reasoning.
q: The comparison employed . . . must be considered rather as a loose analogy than as an exact scientific explanation.

senses.d: Not strict in matters of morality; not rigid according to some standard of right.
q: The loose morality which he had learned.

senses.d: Unconnected; rambling.
q: Vario spends whole mornings in running over loose and unconnected pages.

senses.d: Lax; not costive; having lax bowels.
Dissolute; unchaste; as, a loose man or woman.
q: Loose ladies in delight.

senses.d: Containing or consisting of obscene or unchaste language; as, a loose epistle.

Loose.etym: [OE. loos, lous, laus, Icel. lauss; akin to OD. loos, D. los, AS. leás false, deceitful, G. los, loose, Dan. & Sw. lös, Goth. laus, and E. lose. √127. See Lose, and cf. Leasing falsehood.]

senses.d: Freedom from restraint.
A letting go; discharge.
q: Vent all its griefs, and give a loose to sorrow.

senses.d: To untie or unbind; to free from any fastening; to remove the shackles or fastenings of; to set free; to relieve.
q: Canst thou . . . loose the bands of Orion ?
Ye shall find an ass tied, and a colt with her; loose them, and bring them unto me.

senses.d: To release from anything obligatory or burdensome; to disengage; hence, to absolve; to remit.
q: Art thou loosed from a wife ? seek not a wife.
Whatsoever thou shalt loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven.

senses.d: To relax; to loosen; to make less strict.
q: The joints of his loins were loosed.

senses.d: To solve; to interpret.
To set sail.
A flea.
To cut off as the top or extreme part of anything; to shoorten by cutting off the extremities; to cut off, or remove, as superfluous parts; as, to lop a tree or its branches.
q: Expunge the whole, or lop the excrescent parts.

senses.d: To cut partly off and bend down; as, to lop bushes in a hedge.

Lop.etym: [Prov. G. luppen, lubben,to cut, geld, or OD. luppen, D. lubben.]

senses.d: That which is lopped from anything, as branches from a tree.
To hang downward; to be pendent; to lean to one side.
To let hang down; as, to lop the head.
Hanging down; as, lop ears; — used also in compound adjectives; as, lopeared; lopsided.
A hump-backed person; — so called sportively.
One who has power and authority; a master; a ruler; a governor; a prince; a proprietor, as of a manor.
q: But now I was the lord Of this fair mansion.
Man over men He made not lord.
