senses.d: A titled nobleman., whether a peer of the realm or not; a bishop, as a member of the House of Lords; by courtesy; the son of a duke or marquis, or the eldest son of an earl; in a restricted sense, a baron, as opposed to noblemen of higher rank.
A title bestowed on the persons above named; and also, for honor, on certain official persons; as, lord advocate, lord chamberlain, lord chancellor, lord chief justice, etc.
A husband.
q: Thou worthy lord Of that unworthy wife that greeteth thee.

senses.d: One of whom a fee or estate is held; the male owner of feudal land; as, the lord of the soil; the lord of the manor.
The Supreme Being; Jehovah.
The Savior; Jesus Christ.

Lord.etym: [OE. lord, laverd, loverd, AS. hlāford, for hlāfweard, i.e., bread keeper; hlāf bread, loaf + weardian to look after, to take care of, to ward. See Loaf, and Ward to guard, and cf. Laird, Lady.]

senses.d: To invest with the dignity, power, and privileges of a lord.
To rule or preside over as a lord.
To play the lord; to domineer; to rule with arbitrary or despotic sway; — sometimes with over; and sometimes with it in the manner of a transitive verb.
q: The whiles she lordeth in licentious bliss.
I see them lording it in London streets.
And lorded over them whom now they serve.

senses.d: Suitable for a lord; of or pertaining to a lord; resembling a lord; hence, grand; noble; dignified; honorable.
q: She brought forth butter in a lordly dish.
Lordly sins require lordly estates to support them.
The maidens gathered strength and grace And presence, lordlier than before.

senses.d: Proud; haughty; imperious; insolent.
q: Lords are lordliest in their wine.

Lordly.syn: Imperious; haughty; overbearing; tyrannical; despotic; domineering; arrogant. See Imperious.

senses.d: In a lordly manner.
The state or condition of being a lord; hence (with his or your), a title applied to a lord (except an archbishop or duke, who is called Grace) or a judge (in Great Britain), etc.
Seigniory; domain; the territory over which a lord holds jurisdiction; a manor.
q: What lands and lordships for their owner know My quondam barber.

senses.d: Dominion; power; authority.
q: They which are accounted to rule over the Gentiles exercise lordship over them.

senses.d: Praise. See Loos.

To part with unintentionally or unwillingly, as by accident, misfortune, negligence, penalty, forfeit, etc.; to be deprived of; as, to lose money from one's purse or pocket, or in business or gaming; to lose an arm or a leg by amputation; to lose men in battle.
q: Fair Venus wept the sad disaster Of having lost her favorite dove.

senses.d: To cease to have; to possess no longer; to suffer diminution of; as, to lose one's relish for anything; to lose one's health.
q: If the salt hath lost his savor, wherewith shall it be salted ?

senses.d: Not to employ; to employ ineffectually; to throw away; to waste; to squander; as, to lose a day; to lose the benefits of instruction.
q: The unhappy have but hours, and these they lose.

senses.d: To wander from; to miss, so as not to be able to and; to go astray from; as, to lose one's way.
q: He hath lost his fellows.

senses.d: To ruin; to destroy; as destroy; as, the ship was lost on the ledge.
q: The woman that deliberates is lost.

senses.d: To be deprived of the view of; to cease to see or know the whereabouts of; as, he lost his companion in the crowd.
q: Like following life thro' creatures you dissect, You lose it in the moment you detect.

senses.d: To fail to obtain or enjoy; to fail to gain or win; hence, to fail to catch with the mind or senses; to miss; as, I lost a part of what he said.
q: He shall in no wise lose his reward.
I fought the battle bravely which I lost, And lost it but to Macedonians.

senses.d: To cause to part with; to deprive of.
q: How should you go about to lose him a wife he loves with so much passion ?

senses.d: To prevent from gaining or obtaining.
q: O false heart ! thou hadst almost betrayed me to eternal flames, and lost me this glory.
In the excitement of such a discovery, many scholars lost their heads.

senses.d: To forget or mistake the bearing of surrounding objects; as, to lose one's self in a great city.
To have the perceptive and rational power temporarily suspended; as, we lose ourselves in sleep
To cease to see; as, to lose sight of the land.

Lose.etym: [OE. losien to loose, be lost, lose, AS. losian to become loose; akin to OE. leosen to lose, p. p. loren, lorn, AS. leósan, p. p. loren (in comp.), D. verliezen, G. verlieren, Dan. forlise, Sw. förlisa, förlora, Goth. fraliusan, also to E. loose, a & v., L. luere to loose, Gr. λύειν, Skr. lū to cut.

senses.d: To suffer loss, disadvantage, or defeat; to be worse off, esp. as the result of any kind of contest.
q: We 'll . . . hear poor rogues Talk of court news; and we'll talk with them too, Who loses and who wins; who's in, who's out.

senses.d: The act of losing; failure; destruction; privation; as, the loss of property; loss of money by gaming; loss of health or reputation.
q: Assured loss before the match be played.

senses.d: The state of losing or having lost; the privation, defect, misfortune, harm, etc., which ensues from losing.
q: Though thou repent, yet I have still the loss.

senses.d: That which is lost or from which one has parted; waste; — opposed to gain or increase; as, the loss of liquor by leakage was considerable.
The state of being lost or destroyed; especially, the wreck or foundering of a ship or other vessel.
Failure to gain or win; as, loss of a race or battle.
Failure to use advantageously; as, loss of time.
Killed, wounded, and captured persons, or captured property.

Destruction or diminution of value, if brought about in a manner provided for in the insurance contract (as destruction by fire or wreck, damage by water or smoke), or the death or injury of an insured person; also, the sum paid or payable therefor; as, the losses of the company this year amount to a million of dollars.

Loss.etym: [AS. los loss, losing, fr. leósan to lose. √127. See Lose, v. t.]

senses.d: Parted with unwillingly or unintentionally; not to be found; missing; as, a lost book or sheep.
Parted with; no longer held or possessed; as, a lost limb; lost honor.
Not employed or enjoyed; thrown away; employed ineffectually; wasted; squandered; as, a lost day; a lost opportunity or benefit.
Having wandered from, or unable to find, the way; bewildered; perplexed; as, a child lost in the woods; a stranger lost in London.
Ruined or destroyed, either physically or morally; past help or hope; as, a ship lost at sea; a woman lost to virtue; a lost soul.
Hardened beyond sensibility or recovery; alienated; insensible; as, lost to shame; lost to all sense of honor.
Not perceptible to the senses; no longer visible; as, an island lost in a fog; a person lost in a crowd.
Occupied with, or under the influence of, something, so as to be insensible of external things; as, to be lost in thought.

Lost.etym: [Prop. p. p. of OE. losien. See Lose, v. t.]

senses.d: That which happens without human design or forethought; chance; accident; hazard; fortune; fate.
q: But save my life, which lot before your foot doth lay.

senses.d: Anything (as a die, pebble, ball, or slip of paper) used in determining a question by chance, or without man's choice or will; as, to cast or draw lots.
q: The lot is cast into the lap, but the whole disposing thereof is of the Lord.
If we draw lots, he speeds.

senses.d: The part, or fate, which falls to one, as it were, by chance, or without his planning.
q: O visions ill foreseen! Each day's lot's Enough to bear.
He was but born to try The lot of man — to suffer and to die.

senses.d: A separate portion; a number of things taken collectively; as, a lot of stationery; — colloquially, sometimes of people; as, a sorry lot; a bad lot.
q: I, this winter, met with a very large lot of English heads, chiefly of the reign of James I.

senses.d: A distinct portion or plot of land, usually smaller than a field; as, a building lot in a city.
q: The defendants leased a house and lot in the city of New York.

senses.d: A large quantity or number; a great deal; as, to spend a lot of money; lots of people think so.
q: He wrote to her . . . he might be detained in London by a lot of business.

senses.d: A prize in a lottery.

Lot.etym: [AS. hlot; akin to hleótan to cast lots, OS. hlōt lot, D. lot, G. loos, OHG. lōz, Icel. hlutr, Sw. lott, Dan. lod, Goth. hlauts. Cf. Allot, Lotto, Lottery.]

senses.d: To allot; to sort; to portion.
Having, making, or being a strong or great sound; noisy; striking the ear with great force; as, a loud cry; loud thunder.
q: They were instant with loud voices, requiring that he might be crucified.

senses.d: Clamorous; boisterous.
q: She is loud and stubborn.

senses.d: Emphatic; impressive; urgent; as, a loud call for united effort.
Ostentatious; likely to attract attention; gaudy; as, a loud style of dress; loud colors.

Loud.syn: Noisy; boisterous; vociferous; clamorous; obstreperous; turbulent; blustering; vehement.
Loud.etym: [OE. loud, lud, AS. hlūd; akin to OS. hlūd, D. luid, OHG. lūt, G. laut, L. -clutus, in inclutus, inclitus, celebrated, renowned, cluere to be called, Gr. κλυτόσ heard, loud, famous, κλύειν to hear, Skr. çru. √41. Cf. Client, Listen, Slave a serf.]

senses.d: With loudness; loudly.
q: To speak loud in public assemblies.

senses.d: A feeling of strong attachment induced by that which delights or commands admiration; preëminent kindness or devotion to another; affection; tenderness; as, the love of brothers and sisters.
q: Of all the dearest bonds we prove Thou countest sons' and mothers' love Most sacred, most Thine own.

senses.d: Especially, devoted attachment to, or tender or passionate affection for, one of the opposite sex.
q: He on his side Leaning half-raised, with looks of cordial love Hung over her enamored.

senses.d: Courtship; — chiefly in the phrase to make love, i.e., to court, to woo, to solicit union in marriage.
q: Demetrius . . . Made love to Nedar's daughter, Helena, And won her soul.

senses.d: Affection; kind feeling; friendship; strong liking or desire; fondness; good will; — opposed to hate; often with of and an object.
q: Love, and health to all.
Smit with the love of sacred song.
The love of science faintly warmed his breast.

senses.d: Due gratitude and reverence to God.
q: Keep yourselves in the love of God.

senses.d: The object of affection; — often employed in endearing address.
q: Open the temple gates unto my love.

senses.d: Cupid, the god of love; sometimes, Venus.
q: Such was his form as painters, when they show Their utmost art, on naked Lores bestow.
Therefore do nimble-pinioned doves draw Love.

senses.d: A thin silk stuff.
A climbing species of Clematis (C. Vitalba).
Nothing; no points scored on one side; — used in counting score at tennis, etc.
q: He won the match by three sets to love.

Love.syn: Affection; friendship; kindness; tenderness; fondness; delight.
Love.etym: [OE. love, luve, AS. lufe, lufu; akin to E. lief, believe, L. lubet, libet,it pleases, Skr. lubh to be lustful. See Lief.]

senses.d: To have a feeling of love for; to regard with affection or good will; as, to love one's children and friends; to love one's country; to love one's God.
q: Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind.
Thou shalt love thy neighbor as thy self.

senses.d: To regard with passionate and devoted affection, as that of one sex for the other.
To take delight or pleasure in; to have a strong liking or desire for, or interest in; to be pleased with; to like; as, to love books; to love adventures.
q: Wit, eloquence, and poetry. Arts which I loved.

senses.d: To have the feeling of love; to be in love.
Having such an appearance as excites, or is fitted to excite, love; beautiful; charming; very pleasing in form, looks, tone, or manner.
q: Not one so fair of face, of speech so lovely.
If I had such a tire, this face of mine Were full as lovely as is this of hers.

senses.d: Lovable; amiable; having qualities of any kind which excite, or are fitted to excite, love or friendship.
q: A most lovely gentlemanlike man.

senses.d: Loving; tender.
q: Many a lovely look on them he cast.

senses.d: Very pleasing; — applied loosely to almost anything which is not grand or merely pretty; as, a lovely view; a lovely valley; a lovely melody.
q: Indeed these fields Are lovely, lovelier not the Elysian lawns.

Lovely.syn: Beautiful; charming; delightful; delectable; enchanting; lovable; amiable.

senses.d: In a manner to please, or to excite love.
One who loves; one who is in love; — usually limited, in the singular, to a person of the male sex.
q: Love is blind, and lovers can not see The pretty follies that themselves commit.

senses.d: A friend; one strongly attached to another; one who greatly desires the welfare of any person or thing; as, a lover of his country.
q: I slew my best lover for the good of Rome.

senses.d: One who has a strong liking for anything, as books, science, or music.
Affectionate.
q: The fairest and most loving wife in Greece.

senses.d: Expressing love or kindness; as, loving words.
To make the calling sound of cows and other bovine animals; to moo.
q: The lowing herd wind slowly o'er the lea.

Low.etym: [OE. lowen, AS. hl�wan; akin to D. loeijen, OHG. hl�jan, hluojan.]

senses.d: The calling sound ordinarily made by cows and other bovine animals.
q: Talking voices and the law of herds.

senses.d: A hill; a mound; a grave.

Low.etym: [AS. hlāw; akin to Goth. hlaiw a grave, hlains a hill, and to E. lean to incline.]

senses.d: Fire; a flame; a light.

Low.etym: [Icel. log, logi; akin to E. light, n.]

senses.d: To burn; to blaze.
Occupying an inferior position or place; not high or elevated; depressed in comparison with something else; as, low ground; a low flight.
Not rising to the usual height; as, a man of low stature; a low fence.
Near the horizon; as, the sun is low at four o'clock in winter, and six in summer.
Sunk to the farthest ebb of the tide; as, low tide.
Beneath the usual or remunerative rate or amount, or the ordinary value; moderate; cheap; as, the low price of corn; low wages.
Not loud; as, a low voice; a low sound.
Depressed in the scale of sounds; grave; as, a low pitch; a low note.
Made, as a vowel, with a low position of part of the tongue in relation to the palate; as, ă (ăm), a̤ (a̤ll). See Guide to Pronunciation, §§ 5, 10, 11.
Near, or not very distant from, the equator; as, in the low northern latitudes.
Numerically small; as, a low number.
Wanting strength or animation; depressed; dejected; as, low spirits; low in spirits.
Depressed in condition; humble in rank; as, men of low condition; the lower classes.
q: Why but to keep ye low and ignorant ?

Low.etym: [OE. low, louh, lah, Icel. lāgr; akin to Sw. låg, Dan. lav, D. laag, and E. lie. See Lie to be prostrate.]

senses.d: The lowest trump, usually the deuce; the lowest trump dealt or drawn.
In a low position or manner; not aloft; not on high; near the ground.
Under the usual price; at a moderate price; cheaply; as, he sold his wheat low.
In a low or mean condition; humbly; meanly.
In time approaching our own.
q: In that part of the world which was first inhabited, even as low down as Abraham's time, they wandered with their flocks and herds.

senses.d: With a low voice or sound; not loudly; gently; as, to speak low.
q: The . . . odorous wind Breathes low between the sunset and the moon.

senses.d: With a low musical pitch or tone.
q: Can sing both high and low.

senses.d: In subjection, poverty, or disgrace; as, to be brought low by oppression, by want, or by vice.

In a path near the equator, so that the declination is small, or near the horizon, so that the altitude is small; — said of the heavenly bodies with reference to the diurnal revolution; as, the moon runs low, that is, is comparatively near the horizon when on or near the meridian.
To depress; to lower.
To let descend by its own weight, as something suspended; to let down; as, to lower a bucket into a well; to lower a sail or a boat; sometimes, to pull down; as, to lower a flag.
q: Lowered softly with a threefold cord of love Down to a silent grave.

senses.d: To reduce the height of; as, to lower a fence or wall; to lower a chimney or turret.
To depress as to direction; as, to lower the aim of a gun; to make less elevated as to object; as, to lower one's ambition, aspirations, or hopes.
To reduce the degree, intensity, strength, etc., of; as, to lower the temperature of anything; to lower one's vitality; to lower distilled liquors.
To bring down; to humble; as, to lower one's pride.
To reduce in value, amount, etc.; as, to lower the price of goods, the rate of interest, etc.
To fall; to sink; to grow less; to diminish; to decrease; as, the river lowered as rapidly as it rose.
To be dark, gloomy, and threatening, as clouds; to be covered with dark and threatening clouds, as the sky; to show threatening signs of approach, as a tempest.
q: All the clouds that lowered upon our house.

senses.d: To frown; to look sullen.
q: But sullen discontent sat lowering on her face.

Lower.etym: [OE. lowren, luren; cf. D. loeren, LG. luren. G. lauern to lurk, to be on the watch, and E. leer, lurk.]

senses.d: Cloudiness; gloominess.
A frowning; sullenness.
The calling sound made by cows and other bovine animals.
The state or quality of being lowly; humility; humbleness of mind.
q: Walk . . . with all lowliness and meekness.

senses.d: Low condition, especially as to manner of life.
q: The lowliness of my fortune has not brought me to flatter vice.

senses.d: Not high; not elevated in place; low.
Low in rank or social importance.
q: One common right the great and lowly claims.

senses.d: Not lofty or sublime; humble.
q: These rural poems, and their lowly strain.

senses.d: Having a low esteem of one's own worth; humble; meek; free from pride.
q: Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me, for I am meek and lowly in heart.

senses.d: In a low manner; humbly; meekly; modestly.
In a low condition; meanly.
q: I will show myself highly fed, and lowly taught.

senses.d: A long, narrow spade for stony lands.
The planet Venus, when appearing as the morning star; — applied in Isaiah by a metaphor to a king of Babylon.
q: How art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, son of the morning ! how art thou cut down to the ground which didst weaken the nations !
Tertullian and Gregory the Great understood this passage of Isaiah in reference to the fall of Satan; in consequence of which the name Lucifer has since been applied to Satan.

senses.d: Hence, Satan.
q: How wretched Is that poor man that hangs on princes' favors! . . . When he falls, he falls like Lucifer, Never to hope again.

senses.d: A match made of a sliver of wood tipped with a combustible substance, and ignited by friction; — called also lucifer match, and locofoco. See Locofoco.
A genus of free-swimming macruran Crustacea, having a slender body and long appendages.

Lucifer.etym: [L., bringing light, n., the morning star, fr. lux, lucis, light + ferre to bring.]

senses.d: Gain in money or goods; profit; riches; — often in an ill sense.
q: The lust of lucre and the dread of death.

senses.d: Moderately warm; not hot; tepid.
q: Nine penn'orth o'brandy and water luke.

Luke.etym: [Prob. fr. lew, perh. influenced by AS. wlæc warm, lukewarm, remiss. Cf. Lew.]

senses.d: Moderately warm; neither cold nor hot; tepid; not ardent; not zealous; cool; indifferent.
q: An obedience so lukewarm and languishing that it merits not the name of passion.

senses.d: A small mass of matter of irregular shape; an irregular or shapeless mass; as, a lump of coal; a lump of iron ore.
A mass or aggregation of things.
A projection beneath the breech end of a gun barrel.

Lump.etym: [Cf. OD. lompe piece, mass. Cf. Lunch.]

senses.d: To throw into a mass; to unite in a body or sum without distinction of particulars.
q: The expenses ought to be lumped together.

senses.d: To take in the gross; to speak of collectively.
q: Not forgetting all others, . . . whom for brevity, but out of no resentment to you, I lump all together.

senses.d: To get along with as one can, although displeased; as, if he does n't like it, he can lump it.
To lie hid; to lie in wait.
q: Like wild beasts, lurking in loathsome den.
Let us . . . lurk privily for the innocent.

senses.d: To keep out of sight.
q: The defendant lurks and wanders about in Berks.

Lurk.etym: [OE. lurken, lorken, prob. a dim. from the source of E. lower to frown. See Lower, and cf. Lurch, a sudden roll, Lurch to lurk.]

senses.d: Pleasure.
Inclination; desire.
q: For little lust had she to talk of aught.
My lust to devotion is little.

senses.d: Longing desire; eagerness to possess or enjoy; — in a had sense; as, the lust of gain.
q: The lust of reigning.

senses.d: Licentious craving; sexual appetite.
Hence: Virility; vigor; active power.

Lust.etym: [AS. lust, lust, pleasure, longing; akin to OS., D., G., & Sw. lust, Dan. & Icel. lyst, Goth lustus, and perh. tom Skr. lush to desire, or to E. loose. Cf. List to please, Listless.]

senses.d: To list; to like.
To have an eager, passionate, and especially an inordinate or sinful desire, as for the gratification of the sexual appetite or of covetousness; — often with after.
q: Whatsoever thy soul lusteth after.
Whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her, hath committed adultery with her already in his heart.
The spirit that dwelleth in us lusteth to envy.

Lust.etym: [AS. lystan. See Lust, n., and cf. List to choose.]

senses.d: Exhibiting lust or vigor; stout; strong; vigorous; robust; healthful; able of body.
q: Neither would their old men, so many as were yet vigorous and lusty, be left at home.

senses.d: Beautiful; handsome; pleasant.
Of large size; big. “ Three lusty vessels.” Evelyn. Hence, sometimes, pregnant.
Lustful; lascivious.

Lusty.etym: [From Lust. See Lust, and cf. Luscious.]

senses.d: A bone of the human body which was supposed by certain Rabbinical writers to be indestructible. Its location was a matter of dispute.

Of or pertaining to Lydia, a country of Asia Minor, or to its inhabitants; hence, soft; effeminate; — said especially of one of the ancient Greek modes or keys, the music in which was of a soft, pathetic, or voluptuous character.
q: Softly sweet in Lydian measures, Soon he soothed his soul to pleasures.

senses.d: A strong caustic alkaline solution of potassium salts, obtained by leaching wood ashes. It is much used in making soap, etc.

Lye.etym: [AS. leáh; akin to D. loog, OHG. louga, G. lauge; cf. Icel. laug a bath, a hot spring.]

senses.d: A short side line, connected with the main line; a turn-out; a siding.
A falsehood.
of Lie, to tell a falsehood.
of Lie, to be supported horizontally.
